I’ve been trying to get better at writing film reviews the past few months, and while I think I’ve improved, I still feel like I haven’t found my “voice” or say anything with enough substance.

Here’s my [Letterboxd](https://boxd.it/11JnV) if you want to see some. 

At first I was one of those reviewers that just tried some lame one-liners but that felt cheap and almost degrading towards film as an art form. Then I got more serious, but eventually my writing felt very stagnant and formulaic. Now I’m just trying to keep it more serious, but also write in a more casual tone again. 

What made you all better reviewers? Are there certain things you always touch on in your reviews, or aspects of a movie you focus on and need to critique, whether good or bad?

Also, I noticed that most of my reviews aren’t very critical at all. That’s partially due to me going through my watchlist while sorting it by highest average rating, leading to me thoroughly enjoying a good chunk of them, but I hardly ever negatively criticize the films I watch and I should change that (while not being overly critical and negative, just pointing out minor flaws in the story or whatever.) 

Anyways, what made you a better film reviewer?

Do you read a lot of film criticism?   
If so, do any critics (or film historians, etc.) really speak to you? If so, why? What do they do well? What do they focus on?

That’s a good point, I really don’t honestly. I sometimes read Ebert’s older reviews from before he passed, and occasionally the other reviews on his site from other authors, but I mostly just read reviews on Letterboxd from people I follow who write genuine reviews. 

I should read from some more established writers for sure. I really like how Ebert was great at expressing how he felt about a film in a more creative style rather than the usual comments lower quality blogs will focus on. I love creative writing, so I do eventually want to take inspiration from that down the line. 

Do you have any reviewers you love, or any similar in quality to Roger Ebert? I know that’s a big task since he’s the king of reviews, but I’m more so looking for reviewers with similar styles, not necessarily similar tastes or clout.

My favorite film writers (sometimes a review per se can be very limiting format and you also need to look at essays, histories, etc.)

**Manny Farber**

Rudolf Arnheim 

James Agee

Donald Richie

David Thomson 

Ian Christie 

​

Would also highly, highly recommend filmmakers who are themselves critics and commentators on cinema: Francois Truffaut, Satyajit Ray, Peter Bogdanovich.  
Of course *Hitchcock/Truffaut*.

I do some of my own film writing on a much more amateurish level.

I love a lot of the films in the top 100 but also note some key exclusions. 

I feel like animation and documentaries are especially underrepresented in this list and that it underrates some key films and filmmakers. IE, Steven Spielberg, Walt Disney, Abbas Kiarostami, Joel & Ethan Coen, Preston Sturges, Marcel Carné together have a single film in the top 250.

No *Fantasia* or *Bambi*.

Jean Renoir, unless I'm mistaken, has a single film in the top 400. John Huston doesn't appear until #362. Peter Weir does not make the top 600. Neither Carlos Saura nor Claude Chabrol appear at all. None of the key concert movies like *The Last Waltz*, *Woodstock*, *Monterey Pop* or *Stop Making Sense* make the list. No Erroll Morris, Bill Morrison, Herzog documentaries, etc.

Anyone want to talk Apocalypse Now? I know I'm a bit behind but just saw it and holy shit I haven't felt this way about a movie in a while. I had an idea that it was more out there than your typical war movie but did not expect this.

I guess some random thoughts (Spoilers).

-Kilgore is great, and I think represents the lie of the modern war. He arguably commits as much brutality as Kurtz but it's sanctioned since he does it from a helicopter and treats the locals who survive his onslaught with relative dignity.

-Lance ended up being a surprisingly interesting character. Charmed surfer bro who goes full native and ultimately ends up as one of two sole survivors rather than being punished for his naivety with an untimely death. It seems he has an ability to understand the Jungle like Willard and Kurtz but in a different way. He doesn't resist it or do harm to the locals.
